notes.meaning: When King Hezekiah heard the insulting speech from the Assyrian officer, he tore his clothes and put on rough sackcloth as signs of deep sorrow and humility before God. Instead of calling a council of war or seeking human help, he went straight into the temple courts to pray. He was deeply grieved by the open dishonour done to the name of the living God.

Hezekiah sent his highest royal officials and senior priests, all dressed in sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah. The king sought God's counsel through Isaiah because he knew the prophet spoke the true word of the Lord. In this national emergency, the leaders of the government and the temple stood together in seeking God.

The king described the day as a time of agony, divine correction, and deep shame. He compared Judah to a woman in labour who has reached the moment of birth but has no physical strength left to deliver the child. The nation had exhausted all its human power and would perish unless God stepped in to rescue them.

Hezekiah hoped the Lord would take notice of the Rabshakeh's insults against the living God and answer them. Because the northern tribes had already been taken captive and only a small remnant remained in Judah, he pleaded with Isaiah to pray for those who still survived. His plea was based on protecting God's honour rather than claiming any goodness in the people.
The royal officers carried out Hezekiah's command and delivered the king's message faithfully to Isaiah. They placed their desperate situation directly before God's chosen messenger.

Isaiah told the messengers to tell Hezekiah not to fear the threats of the Assyrian officers. The Lord took the insults personally, explaining that these men had blasphemed Him, not merely threatened Jerusalem. God referred to these mighty officials with a belittling term, showing they were merely young attendants compared to the Almighty.

The Lord promised to intervene by placing an impulse within Sennacherib so that he would hear a troubling report and pull back to his homeland. There in Assyria, God would cause him to die by the sword. A simple breath or decree from God would undo all the terrifying power of the invader.

The Rabshakeh pulled back from Jerusalem and discovered that Sennacherib had moved on from Lachish to attack the nearby fortress of Libnah. He went to rejoin his king to report on his mission and receive further orders.

Sennacherib received word that King Tirhakah of Cush was marching north to fight against him. Needing to secure Jerusalem quickly to protect his rear before this new battle began, Sennacherib sent another threatening message to Hezekiah to force a quick surrender.

The message warned Hezekiah not to let his trust in God fool him into thinking Jerusalem was safe from the Assyrian army. Sennacherib directly challenged God's truthfulness, claiming the Lord was promising something He could not deliver.

Sennacherib boasted of how previous Assyrian kings had wiped out entire nations, asking why Hezekiah expected to be spared. He listed conquered regions and cities such as Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, Hamath, and Arpad, arguing that their gods and kings had completely failed to protect them. By doing this, he treated the living God as if He were just another helpless idol.

Hezekiah took the threatening letter from the messengers, read it, and carried it straight into the temple courts. He spread it out before the Lord, openly laying the problem and its blasphemies before God's eyes in prayer.

Hezekiah began his prayer by worshipping the Lord as the God of Israel who sits enthroned above the cherubim on the ark of the covenant. He declared that the Lord alone rules over every kingdom on earth because He created both heaven and earth. Unlike the localized idols the Assyrians conquered, God is the supreme Master of everything.

Hezekiah pleaded with God to listen closely and look upon the written arrogance sent by Sennacherib. He stressed that the enemy's insults were not simply attacks on Judah, but open defiance against the living God.

The king admitted that Assyria had truly destroyed many lands and burned their idols in the fire. However, he pointed out that those supposed deities were not real gods at all, but merely wood and stone carved by human hands. Their destruction proved the weakness of man-made idols, not any weakness in the Creator.

Hezekiah begged the Lord to rescue Judah from Sennacherib's hand so that all nations across the earth would know that the Lord alone is the true God. His chief desire was not merely personal survival, but that God's name and glory would be made famous everywhere.

Isaiah sent word to Hezekiah that the Lord had heard his prayer about Sennacherib. God gave the answer by direct revelation to the prophet while the king was still praying. The rescue that followed was God's direct response to Hezekiah's humble cry.

God answered Sennacherib by picturing Jerusalem as an untouched virgin daughter who laughed at him and shook her head in mockery. Though Sennacherib thought he would conquer the city with ease, Jerusalem remained safe under the protective care of her heavenly Father.

The Lord challenged the Assyrian king by asking whom he thought he was insulting with his proud words and arrogant looks. Sennacherib had lifted himself up against the Holy One of Israel, whose pure majesty and power could never be mocked without consequence.

God quoted Sennacherib's inner boasts back to him. The Assyrian king bragged that his vast fleets of chariots could scale the highest peaks of Lebanon, cutting down its finest cedars and cypress trees to conquer every frontier. He thought no natural barrier could slow his army down.

The invader went on boasting that he could dig wells in dry deserts and that his vast armies could dry up the rivers of Egypt just by marching across them. He fancied that he had absolute power over nature and every river in the lands he meant to invade.

The Lord answered this pride by asking if Sennacherib had failed to understand that God had planned all these events long ago. Assyria was merely an instrument in God's hands to carry out His judgments and turn fortified cities into ruins.

The conquered nations were helpless and frightened because God had taken away their strength. They were as frail as tender grass or green shoots on a rooftop, which quickly wither in the hot sun before they can even grow.

God declared that He knew every move Sennacherib made, whether sitting at home, marching out to battle, or raging against the Lord. Nothing the king thought or planned was hidden from the Lord's sight.

Because of Sennacherib's furious rebellion and arrogance, God promised to handle him like a wild animal. The Lord would put a hook in his nose and a bit in his mouth, forcing him to march back home by the exact route he had come.

The Lord gave Hezekiah a reassuring sign about their food supply. The Assyrian invasion had ruined the farming season, but for two years the people would have enough to eat from wild crops and natural growth, until regular planting and harvesting fully resumed in the third year. This provided visible proof that God had truly broken the enemy's grip.

Just like crops taking deep root and yielding an abundant harvest, the surviving people of Judah would flourish again. They would establish themselves securely in their towns and multiply after the long devastation of war.

A surviving remnant would spread out from Jerusalem and Mount Zion to repopulate the land. The Lord's fierce, passionate commitment to His people and His promises would guarantee that this restoration took place.

The Lord promised that the king of Assyria would not step foot inside Jerusalem or even shoot a single arrow over its walls. His soldiers would not bring shields before the gates or build dirt ramps to attack the city.
Sennacherib would turn back along the very road he traveled to get there, leaving the holy city untouched. The Lord's decree settled the matter completely.

God pledged to shelter and defend Jerusalem for the honour of His own name and because of the covenant promise He had made to King David. Deliverance came not from Judah's merit, but from God's faithfulness to His Word.

That very night, the angel of the Lord struck down 185,000 soldiers in the Assyrian camp. When the survivors woke up the following morning, they looked out upon fields covered with dead bodies. God saved Jerusalem without His people needing to fight a single battle.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Historians often compare this event to an account in Herodotus reporting that a plague carried by field mice suddenly ruined the Assyrian army near Egypt.

notes.meaning: Crushed and humiliated, Sennacherib broke camp immediately and retreated to Assyria. He settled back in his capital city of Nineveh and never launched another military campaign against Jerusalem.

Later, while Sennacherib was bowing down to worship inside the temple of his idol Nisroch, two of his own sons struck him down with the sword. The murderers escaped into the mountains of Ararat, and another son named Esar-haddon took over the throne, fulfilling God's earlier promise that the proud king would fall by the sword in his own land.
